vignette: Kofi is a 23-year-old African American male working as an urban planner in Chicago. He has been single since his traumatic assault two years ago that left him deeply shaken and struggling to navigate daily life. The night of the assault was particularly vivid for Kofi. He had gone out with friends, and they stopped at a bar where someone was drunk and threw bottles aggressively while yelling loudly. The chaos escalated quickly, leading to an altercation where he was physically assaulted. The smell of alcohol in that bar has since been seared into his memory as a potent trigger. Kofi now finds himself reacting strongly to any expressions of anger from others, even if they are calm. This often leads him to self-blame and rumination. "I dwell on what I have done wrong," he says. He also turns to gambling for distraction or excitement when these triggers emerge. "It’s the only thing that makes me feel like I’m in control." The assault has made Kofi overly sensitive to sudden movements and sounds. A simple clatter of dishes or a quick gesture can cause him to react as if he were back in danger, unable to believe others’ reassurances about his safety. This heightened state of alertness often leads him to avoid any potential conflicts at work, where disagreements could arise over urban development projects. Kofi remembers the traumatic event as a series of snapshots that flood his mind at unexpected moments. Each picture is vivid and overwhelming with emotion, making it difficult for him to find words to describe what happened. "I know what happened but I am unable to find words," he explains. The memories are so intense that they prompt him to gamble or ruminate deeply on his failures. Kofi’s experiences have also led him to believe that the institutions and people meant to protect him failed him, exacerbating his feelings of helplessness. "I can't stop bad things from happening to me," he says. This belief makes it hard for him to cope with any form of stress, even minor upsets at work. One instance where this became clear was during a city council meeting where an angry protester threw a cup and shouted in frustration. Kofi’s reaction was immediate—he felt like he couldn’t breathe, and his mind flooded with images from the assault. He had to leave abruptly, only adding to his self-blame and feeling of helplessness. Kofi's negative appraisals have also led him to engage more frequently in maladaptive strategies such as gambling or avoiding conflict altogether. "Even when others tell me I am safe, I find it impossible to believe it," he admits, reinforcing his reliance on these coping mechanisms that provide temporary relief but worsen the cycle. The accumulation of these behaviors has strained Kofi’s professional relationships and ability to perform effectively at work. He avoids meetings or public forums where conflict might arise, leading him to miss critical opportunities for collaboration and progress in urban planning projects. What finally brought Kofi to seek help was a realization that his life had become unmanageable. "I couldn't deal with even the slightest upset," he says, referring to the overwhelming nature of his emotions and triggers. He is most hopeful that therapy might offer him new ways to cope and regain a sense of control over his life. Kofi’s current state reflects a complex web of interlinked symptoms where each component feeds into the others, forming a self-reinforcing cycle. His fears are palpable as he struggles with both the immediate effects of his triggers and the long-term consequences on his mental health and professional life.
